science.title: Neural cellular automata approach for reducing security and privacy hazards of augmented reality environment
science.description: The applications of the Augmented Reality (AR) environment are getting traction in the field of healthcare, smart city navigation, and industrial training and collaboration working environments. Nevertheless, this constant streaming of multimedia and the exchange of sensor information may subject the security and privacy threat of illegitimate access, data capture, and inference. Unlike prior AR frameworks, the proposed study incorporates a novel Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) layer that actively learns AR behavior and dynamically enforces spatial-temporal anomaly detection, adaptive access control and encryption. The proposed NCA layer leverages the localized state evaluation to define the spatial dependence and distributed behavioral pattern in the AR stream. The NCA layer defines rules for each stream and monitors the AR environment activities elegantly, anomaly detection with adaptive neural models, in its dynamic access decision. The layer further incorporated with an optimized key generation algorithm on a symmetric encryption technique to ensure secure transmission with minimal computational overhead. The experimental results of the proposed study show the intrusion detection rate is 96.8%, access control decision accuracy is 94.3%, and the overhead of encryption was below 6%. Analysis of a deployment in the post-deployment stage indicated that this multi-layered mechanism of privacy lessened measurable AR security and privacy risk by more than 85% in simulated attack conditions.

science.title: Complex IV inhibitors reprogram root growth and induce mitophagy in Arabidopsis
science.description: Electrons harvested from food are carried to the electron transport chain (ETC) to drive cellular energy production. The rate-limiting enzyme of mitochondrial ETC (mtETC/mETC) is cytochrome c oxidase (CcO)/Complex IV. Complex IV deficiency leads to severe human diseases and plant lethality, yet how Complex IV inhibition affects mitochondrial dynamics and cellular homeostasis remains unclear. Using two thiamine pyrophosphate-thiazole (TPP thiazole, TPPT) derivatives that specifically target mitochondria and reversibly inhibit Complex IV, we show that TPPT treatment inhibits primary root growth in Arabidopsis in an auxin- and ATP-dependent manner. Furthermore, moderate TPPT treatment leads to partial depolarization of mitochondria and induces autophagy and mitophagy, whereas excessive TPPT disrupts vacuolar dynamics and inhibits mitophagy. In summary, TPPT derivatives as mild Complex IV inhibitors are useful tools for dissecting cellular remodeling upon energy deficiency and for the study of mitophagy. A study uses reversible Complex IV inhibitors (TPPT) to investigate how mitochondrial inhibition affects root growth, endomembrane trafficking, and mitophagy in Arabidopsis, finding that TPPT has dose-dependent effects on mitochondrial function and degradation, inducing both macro- and micro-mitophagy.

science.title: Hydrogen-helium immiscibility boundary in gas-giant planetary interiors from machine-learning molecular dynamics
science.description: The location of the hydrogen-helium (H/He) immiscibility boundary controls whether and where helium rain occurs in giant planets, yet it remains uncertain because high-pressure experiments are challenging and ab initio simulations are limited in system size and simulation time. We map this boundary by computing composition-dependent chemical potentials from large-scale molecular dynamics driven by machine learning potentials trained on three density functional approximations (PBE, vdW-DF, and the hybrid HSE). Across the pressure range of 100-1000 GPa, the demixing temperatures are typically  ~ 2000 K lower than previous ab initio simulations using small system sizes, and this discrepancy is larger than the estimated error from the chosen density functionals, machine learning potentials, neglect of nuclear quantum effects, and statistical uncertainties. Fitting the H/He mixing free energy to a Redlich-Kister regular solution model rationalizes the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation, and provides a predictive representation of the boundary. Comparing with current planetary interior profiles indicates that helium rain is plausible in Saturn but unlikely in the warmer interior of Jupiter. Our results narrow the uncertainty in the H/He immiscibility boundary and provide inputs for planetary models that couple demixing, heat transport, and composition gradients in gas giants. The authors use machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations to map the hydrogen-helium immiscibility boundary under gas-giant interior conditions, constraining models of planetary structure and evolution.
